summary: This standards-track memo registers the text/red MIME sub-type. Red stands for redundant. The actual RTP packetisation for the type is given in RFC 2198.

eli5.summary: This gives an official name to a way of sending text with backup copies so lost packets can be recovered.

questions: what is redundant text in rtp
what is the text red mime type
how does text/red map to sdp
what are the rate and pt parameters in text/red
subtitle: The registration that gives redundant real-time text its official MIME name, text/red.

tldr.problem: Real-time text sent over RTP can benefit from redundancy, but the redundant format needed an official MIME sub-type name that tools such as SDP could use.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers text/red with two required parameters, rate and pt, and explains how those map onto SDP lines. The actual packet format stays in RFC 2198.
tldr.outcome: text/red is defined only for transfer over RTP, never as a storage format. The memo is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6354.

facts.label: Usage restriction
facts.value: RTP transfer only, not a storage format

today: RFC 4102 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6354, so read the two together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Text Needs a Redundancy Type
sections.content:
Text is an important part of any multimedia communication system. Like audio, text transport can use redundancy to improve reliability and the end-user experience. In the name red, the word is short for redundant.

RFC 2198 already defines an RTP payload format for redundant audio data, and the memo notes that the same format suits text too. RFC 4103 specifies one use of that format and of the text/red MIME type for redundant text.

This memo only supplies the MIME sub-type registration. It focuses on use in SDP, but says the type is not restricted to SDP.
sections.eli5: If you say something twice, a friend who missed it the first time can still catch it. This memo just writes down the official name for text sent that way.

sections.title: The text/red Registration and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The registration is for media type name text and subtype name RED. It has two required parameters.

  • rate: the RTP clock rate of the payload. Typically this is 1000, but other rates MAY be specified. It MUST equal the clock rate of the text payload format carried as the primary encoding.
  • pt: a comma-separated, ordered list of RTP payload types naming the primary, secondary and later encodings, as in RFC 2198. Because a comma is a special character, the list MUST be a quoted-string.

For static payload types each list element is just the type number. For dynamic payload types each element maps the payload type number to an embedded MIME content-type, written as dynamic-payload-type "=" content-type. Quotation marks inside the quoted list MUST be escaped with backslash quoting as in RFC 2045, applied recursively if the content-type itself contains a quoted-string.

The optional parameters are ptime and maxptime, defined originally in RFC 2327 and RFC 3267.
sections.eli5: The name tag has two blanks to fill in: how fast the clock ticks, and a list saying which kinds of text are the main copy and which are the spare copies.

sections.title: Restrictions and Registration Details
sections.content:
The type is defined only for transfer via RTP. It shall not be defined for a storage format, so the encoding considerations simply point back to this restriction, as RFC 3555 requires.

The registration lists the published specification as RFC 2198, the intended usage as COMMON, and the applications as text streaming and conferencing tools. It reports no interoperability considerations. The change controller is the AVT Working Group, delegated from the IESG.
sections.eli5: This kind of text is meant to be sent live over the network, not saved in a file.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) is commonly used to describe RTP sessions, and the memo spells out where each piece of the MIME registration goes.

  • The MIME type text goes in the SDP m= line as the media name.
  • rate goes in a=rtpmap, and the subtype RED goes there as the encoding name.
  • ptime and maxptime go in the a=ptime and a=maxptime attributes.
  • pt becomes an a=fmtp attribute: drop the parameter name and change the commas to slashes. The number of elements in the list shows the level of redundancy.

Any dynamic payload type in the list MUST be written as its number, not its content-type; the number-to-type mapping is done with normal SDP a=rtpmap lines. For each redundancy payload type the ordering of primary and redundancy encodings is fixed, so wanting more than one combination means defining more than one redundancy payload type.
sections.eli5: When two programs set up a call, they write a little note describing it. This part says which line of the note holds which piece of the text/red name tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2198 apply. The memo adds that text data, perhaps even more than audio, is susceptible to unwanted modification that may lead to undesired results.

To prevent modification of the primary data, the secondary data or the header information, payload integrity protection over at least the complete RTP packet is RECOMMENDED, for example using SRTP.
sections.eli5: Someone could sneak in and change the words on the way. Putting a tamper-proof seal on the whole package stops that.

data.title: SDP using text/red
data.code:
m=text 11000 RTP/AVP 98 100
a=rtpmap:98 t140/1000
a=rtpmap:100 red/1000
a=fmtp:100 98/98
